text:
The U.N. nuclear watchdog on Thursday released its first report on Korea's project to build nuclear-powered submarines, expressing satisfaction over related cooperation with the Asian country, according to Seoul's foreign ministry.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) issued the report, titled "Naval Nuclear Propulsion: Republic of Korea," under the name of Director General Rafael Grossi as it discussed the report during its Board of Governors' meeting in Vienna this week.
The report came as Korea and the IAEA have begun consultations on safeguards and other matters related to the submarine project. The IAEA has been issuing annual reports on Australia and Brazil since 2022 and 2023, respectively, as the two countries have been in consultation with the agency over their submarine projects.
The IAEA assessed in the report that Seoul has implemented its reporting obligations under the Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement (CSA) and the Additional Protocol (AP), the ministry said, noting the agency has maintained the "broad conclusion" since 2007 that all nuclear materials in Korea have been used for peaceful activities.
A CSA is an agreement between a non-nuclear-weapon state and the IAEA under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), aimed at ensuring all nuclear materials used by the state for peaceful purposes are not diverted to nuclear weapons. The AP is an additional pact meant to strengthen the IAEA's verification capabilities.
The IAEA expressed its satisfaction over technical consultations and other exchanges with Seoul over the submarine project, while hoping bilateral engagement will continue to ensure that Korea continues to abide by its non-proliferation and safeguard commitments, the ministry said.
"The (Korean) government plans to continue technical consultations with the IAEA under the principle of faithfully fulfilling nuclear non-proliferation and IAEA safeguard obligations during the process of developing and operating nuclear-powered submarines, and maintaining transparent and close communication with the IAEA," the ministry said.
Korea seeks to acquire nuclear-powered, conventionally armed attack submarines as the United States agreed in a joint document last year to cooperate in meeting requirements for the project, including sourcing fuel to power the strategic vessels.
